draft.title: Vaccination
card: A vaccine contains a harmless form or part of a pathogen. It may be a weakened or killed pathogen, or a piece of one, such as a protein.
The vaccine carries antigens, so the immune system responds to it. B cells and T cells are activated, and some become memory cells.
Memory cells stay in the body for a long time. The person gets no illness from the first exposure, because the vaccine cannot cause the disease.
If the real pathogen enters later, memory cells respond faster and more strongly than in a first infection. This stops or reduces the disease.
draft.remember: A vaccine trains the immune system with antigens, so memory cells are ready before the real pathogen arrives.

a.q: Why does a vaccine let a person become immune without getting the disease?
opts: It carries antigens that cause memory cells to form
It contains antibodies that kill the pathogen later
It contains antibiotics that destroy the pathogen
It stops the pathogen from ever entering the body
a.why: The vaccine's antigens trigger an immune response, and memory cells form without the pathogen causing illness. Giving antibodies is a tempting idea, but the vaccine works by making the body build its own response and memory.
a.clue: Think about what the immune system needs to recognise.

b.q: Priya is vaccinated with a vaccine made from one protein of a virus. Months later she is exposed to the whole virus. Why is her illness likely to be mild or absent?
opts: Memory cells for that protein respond quickly to the virus
The protein she received has already killed the virus
The vaccine made her body stop making new cells to infect
She now has a first-time response that is slow but strong
b.why: The protein acted as an antigen, so memory cells formed. When the virus has the same protein, those cells respond faster and more strongly. A slow first-time response is wrong, because that is what happens without earlier exposure.
b.clue: The viral protein in the vaccine is also found on the virus.

a.best: It carries antigens that cause memory cells to form

b.best: Memory cells for that protein respond quickly to the virus

problems.detail: The card says the vaccine 'cannot cause the disease', but it also lists weakened (live attenuated) pathogens. These can rarely cause illness, for example vaccine-derived polio from the oral polio vaccine, or disease in people with weak immune systems. They can also cause mild symptoms. Safer wording: 'the vaccine is very unlikely to cause the disease' or 'is designed not to cause the disease'.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer, and the explanations match the card. The card's claim that a vaccine 'cannot cause the disease' is too absolute for weakened live vaccines and should be softened.
